text: You've probably heard that AI just predicts the next word.
That's true.
But it's also where most explanations stop.
In September 2024, OpenAI tested two of its models on the AIME,
a hard American math competition.
The older model, GPT-4o, solved about 12 percent of the problems.
The newer one, called o1, solved 74 percent.
Both of them still work by predicting the next word.
The difference is that one of them learned to think before it answers.
Let's start with what the model actually sees.
Not letters. Not words. Numbers.
Your text gets chopped into pieces called tokens.
In English, a token is about four characters,
or roughly three quarters of a word.
Each token is then swapped for an ID number.
From here on, the model never sees your words again.
Only these numbers.
That's why AI can stumble on things that feel trivial to us,
like counting the letters in a word.
It never saw the letters.
So what does the model do with those numbers?
Just one job, over and over:
given everything so far, what comes next?
For every possible next token, it gives a probability.
After "The cat sat on the," the word "mat" might score high,
"floor" a bit lower, and "banana" almost zero.
It picks one, adds it to the end, and asks the same question again.
Token by token,
that's how every answer you've ever gotten from a chatbot was built.
A long answer can take hundreds or even thousands of these predictions,
each one depending on everything that came before it.
And it doesn't always pick the top choice.
A little randomness is usually built in,
which is why the same question can get two different answers.
So far, this is the explanation you've heard before.
The interesting part is where those probabilities come from.
Inside the model are billions of numbers called parameters.
GPT-3, back in 2020, had 175 billion of them.
So how does it decide which earlier words matter?
Inside, each token becomes a long list of numbers,
and those lists pass through layer after layer.
In each layer, every token can look back at the tokens before it,
and pull in the ones that are relevant.
Take this sentence: "The cat sat on the mat because it was tired."
To make sense of "it," the model has to connect it back to "cat," not "mat."
This step is called attention.
It comes from a 2017 paper by researchers at Google,
titled "Attention Is All You Need,"
and it's the core of the design behind today's large language models.
At the start, all those parameters are random,
and the model's guesses are nonsense.
Training is a guessing game.
Show the model real text, hide the next token, let it guess,
then nudge every parameter slightly toward the right answer.
Then do it again. And again.
Meta's Llama 3 was trained on more than 15 trillion tokens.
To put that in perspective:
a person reading nonstop, at an average reading speed,
would need roughly 90,000 years to get through that much text.
And here's the surprising part.
To get good at guessing the next word across all that text,
the model ends up picking up grammar, facts,
and patterns of reasoning along the way.
Nobody programmed those in.
They're a side effect of getting good at guessing.
But a model trained only this way has a strange problem.
It's an autocomplete for the internet.
Ask it a question, and it might just write more questions,
the way a quiz or a homework sheet would carry on.
Turning it into an assistant takes a second, much smaller round of training.
People write example answers and rank the model's replies,
and the model is tuned toward the ones people prefer.
Ranking is the clever part.
It's much easier for a person to say which of two answers is better
than to write the perfect answer themselves.
In 2022, OpenAI showed how powerful this step is.
People preferred answers from a 1.3 billion parameter model trained this way
over the 175 billion parameter GPT-3.
A model more than 100 times smaller, and people liked it better.
By 2023, that was the full story:
predict the next word, then get polished by human feedback.
Then the story changed.
Remember those math scores?
12 percent versus 74.
The key new ingredient was a different kind of training,
called reinforcement learning.
OpenAI hasn't published the details,
but here's the basic idea, as other labs have since described it.
Give the model a math problem.
Let it write out as much working as it wants before its final answer.
If the answer is right, reward it.
If it's wrong, don't.
Nobody shows it how to reason.
It only finds out whether it got the answer right.
In January 2025, the Chinese lab DeepSeek published
what happened when they trained a model this way.
On that same math competition,
the model's score climbed from 15.6 percent to 71 percent
over the course of training.
And it started doing things nobody had taught it.
It spent longer thinking on each problem.
It went back and checked its own steps.
At one point, in the middle of a solution, it wrote:
"Wait, wait. Wait."
Then it found its own mistake.
The researchers called it an "aha moment."
By the spring of 2025, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Anthropic and Google
had all released models that can think before they answer.
And OpenAI reported something else:
the longer the model is allowed to think, the better it tends to do.
That's what is happening when a chatbot pauses
and shows you a "thinking" label.
It's writing out its working before it shows you the answer.
And that working isn't free.
Every thinking token has to be predicted, just like the answer.
On OpenAI's API, those reasoning tokens are billed as output,
even though you never see them.
That's why thinking mode is slower,
and why it often costs more.
So here's the part most explanations miss.
AI still just predicts the next word.
That never changed.
What changed is what it's predicting.
Not just what someone on the internet would write next,
but the steps that lead to a right answer.
The thinking is made of the same tokens, one at a time.
It's next-word prediction, pointed at a goal.
So the whole recipe has three stages.
First, guess the next word across trillions of tokens.
Second, get polished by human preferences.
Third, get rewarded for reaching right answers.
Most explanations stop after the first two.
The third is the one that changed what AI can do.
What does this mean for you?
First, for hard problems, like math, code, or planning,
use the thinking mode if your AI has one.
It's the same kind of machine, given time to think.
Second, thinking isn't the same as knowing.
Its knowledge still comes from patterns in its training,
so it can reason carefully and still be wrong.
Check anything that matters.
So here's my question.
When an AI writes "wait, let me check that," is it really thinking?
Or is it just a very good prediction of what thinking looks like?
Tell me in the comments.
